clinicalPearls: A congenital myopathy defined by multiple small cores (minicores) lacking oxidative enzyme activity, most often caused by recessive variants in SELENON (SEPN1) or RYR1

The classic SELENON-related form features axial and neck weakness, early spinal rigidity, scoliosis, and prominent respiratory muscle involvement, sometimes with respiratory failure while ambulation is preserved
RYR1-related forms may show more limb-girdle weakness, external ophthalmoplegia, or overlap with core and centronuclear myopathies
RYR1-related disease carries a risk of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, so anaesthetic precautions are essential
Onset is typically in infancy or early childhood with hypotonia and delayed motor milestones, and progression is usually slow
Creatine kinase is normal or only mildly elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern
Muscle biopsy shows multiple small cores of reduced oxidative staining that do not extend the length of the fibre, distinguishing them from the long central cores of central core disease
Diagnosis integrates the minicore biopsy findings, clinical phenotype, and SELENON or RYR1 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Multiminicore disease is a genetically heterogeneous congenital myopathy. SELENON encodes selenoprotein N, an endoplasmic reticulum protein involved in redox regulation and calcium handling, and its loss impairs protection against oxidative stress and calcium homeostasis in muscle. RYR1 encodes the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor, the calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum central to excitation-contraction coupling; variants disturb calcium release and can also confer malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. In both, focal areas of mitochondrial depletion and disrupted oxidative metabolism form the multiple minicores seen histologically, and the resulting impaired contraction produces weakness, with axial and respiratory muscles particularly affected in the SELENON-related form.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital myopathies (centronuclear, nemaline, congenital fibre-type disproportion)
Congenital muscular dystrophy including rigid spine syndrome
Spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of infantile hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme histochemistry and electron microscopy to demonstrate minicores
Muscle MRI to define the pattern of muscle involvement
Respiratory function testing including lying and sitting vital capacity, given the risk of respiratory failure
Genetic testing of SELENON and RYR1 and a broader congenital myopathy panel
redFlags: Respiratory insufficiency or nocturnal hypoventilation, which can occur even in ambulant patients
Progressive scoliosis or spinal rigidity compromising respiration
Personal or family history of adverse anaesthetic reaction suggesting malignant hyperthermia in RYR1 disease
Rapid deterioration atypical for a slowly progressive congenital myopathy
reference.prognosis: Many patients remain ambulant with slow progression, but respiratory muscle involvement, especially in the SELENON-related form, can lead to ventilatory failure requiring support and is a major determinant of prognosis; proactive respiratory and orthopaedic surveillance improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Failing to monitor respiratory function because limb strength and walking are relatively preserved
Overlooking malignant hyperthermia susceptibility in RYR1-related disease when planning anaesthesia
Not flagging avoidance of volatile anaesthetic agents and depolarising muscle relaxants and ensuring dantrolene availability where RYR1 variants are implicated
Confusing minicores with the long central cores of central core disease on biopsy
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
GeneReviews: Multiminicore disease and RYR1-related myopathies
management: Proactive respiratory surveillance with lying and sitting vital capacity and nocturnal non-invasive ventilation for respiratory muscle weakness
Orthopaedic management of scoliosis and spinal rigidity, including bracing and spinal fusion where indicated
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain mobility and prevent contractures
Malignant hyperthermia precautions in RYR1-related disease, avoiding volatile anaesthetics and depolarising muscle relaxants and using total intravenous anaesthesia
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular care coordinating neurology, respiratory medicine, orthopaedics and physiotherapy
Genetic counselling and family testing that accounts for recessive SELENON and dominant or recessive RYR1 inheritance
Escalate respiratory support as ventilatory function declines, since respiratory failure is the main determinant of prognosis
